agent.problem: The blank asks the baker to recover an unseen object from the verse. The earlier cards establish the urgency of fleeing, but nothing in them makes "cloak" a more reasoned choice than "sandals" or "staff"; the object could be swapped without changing the point about not going back. This tests wording rather than a meaning the baker can infer.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

human.problem: This joke is the same comparison as stop 1, card 6: a scam message that looks official but is fake ("sounds official, is NOT" and then "looks real, is NOT your bank"). The same image and punchline shape come back in one walkthrough. The docs say there's no formula, but they don't say whether a comparison can be reused within a lesson.
human.question: Should Papa Dorin avoid reusing the same comparison or punchline shape within one walkthrough, even when the passage repeats its theme (here, deception in Mark 13:6 and 13:22)?

human.problem: The last story card is only the "story isn't over" line, but it cites Mark 13:23. It tells nothing from 13:23. Its only Bible detail, Jesus sitting on the mountain, comes from Mark 13:3. The docs allow this card to be just the line when the last verse was asked on a choice card, but they don't say what it should cite.
human.question: What should a closing card cite when it is only the "story isn't over" line: the passage's last verse, the verse its detail comes from (here Mark 13:3), or no verses at all?
